title: Just a Teacher
author: Harriett Janetos
summary: Harriett Janetos describes how expert feedback on her reading guide left her feeling like just a teacher, and how Steve Dykstra's reminder that scientists do not know what teachers know restored her confidence. She explains her diagram pairing Scarborough's Reading Rope, which describes the components of skilled reading, with the Four-Part Processing Model, which shows how the brain integrates them and so directs instruction. Her broader argument is that research should be weighed against classroom experience and that teachers should resist trends and those promoting them until they have considered their own context. She closes by quoting Bronwyn Ryrie Jones on platforming people who know the craft of teaching.
points: Janetos distinguishes the Rope as descriptive and the Four-Part Processing Model as directive, and argues instruction fails when components are marched through without integration.
Dykstra's point that scientists and teachers each hold knowledge the other lacks gave her licence to keep choices she had thought through.
Her advice is to evaluate evidence in light of your own classroom and resist trends until they are shown to fit your context.
Teachers are experienced practitioners melding research with daily interaction with students, not mere implementers of expert views.
quotes: It may help to view one as descriptive, the other as directive. The Rope describes the literacy elements necessary for skilled reading, and the Model describes how the brain uses those elements to achieve that goal, thereby directing effective instruction.

Reading instruction fails when we march through literacy components (If it’s Tuesday, it must be . . .) without careful consideration for how to integrate these components—how to make the strands of the reading rope make sense in the reader’s brain by uniting letters, sounds, and meanings.
Dykstra was right, of course. I wasn’t just a teacher, I was an experienced teacher trying to follow the research by melding it with my day-to-day interactions with students.
Evaluate the evidence in light of your own experiences, and resist the trends and the people promoting those trends until you’ve considered how the research relates to your own classroom context.

My humble advice is to be careful not to fall into the trend trap and steadfastly resist the pull from those professing to have answers if they haven’t demonstrated to you that they’ve been asking all the right questions within the context of the classroom.

I’m optimistic that a cultural course correction is possible. We’ll know it’s happening when we platform the people who’ve done the hard yards on curriculum, who’ve implemented explicit teaching in classrooms with actual children in them, who know teaching because they really know the craft.
